title: Factorial Experiments: Main Effects and Interactions
breadcrumb: Unit III · Design of Experiments · Factorial layouts
objectives: Explain why factorial experiments study two or more factors simultaneously.
Construct and interpret treatment combinations in a 2² and 2³ factorial experiment.
Calculate main effects and interaction effects using marginal means and contrasts.
Partition the treatment sum of squares into orthogonal factorial components in a balanced replicated 2² experiment.
Distinguish replication, randomisation and interaction, and interpret interaction before marginal main effects.

traps: A factorial experiment studies all combinations of the selected factor levels; it is not merely several separate one-factor experiments.
A main effect is an average effect over the levels of the other factor(s).
An interaction means the effect of one factor changes across levels of another factor.
When interaction is substantial, report simple effects or cell means; a marginal main effect can hide different or reversed responses.
For a full 2^k factorial there are 2^k treatment combinations and 2^k−1 non-empty factorial effects.
Replication means independently applying the same treatment combination to multiple experimental units; repeated readings on one unit are not automatically independent replications.
Orthogonality of factorial contrasts in a balanced design does not remove the need for randomisation.
howto: Begin with the treatment-combination table. Mark low and high levels, compute cell means, then calculate marginal main effects and difference-in-differences interactions. For ANOVA, write the effect degrees of freedom before calculating mean squares. Complete the mastery test without hints.

sheet: A factorial experiment studies all combinations of levels of two or more factors.
A 2² design has 4 combinations; a 2³ design has 8 combinations.
For 2²: A−B−, A+B−, A−B+, A+B+; each factor has low (−) and high (+) levels.
Main effect A = mean response at A+ − mean response at A−, averaged over B.
Main effect B = mean response at B+ − mean response at B−, averaged over A.
AB interaction = [A effect at B+] − [A effect at B−], equivalently a difference-in-differences.
In a replicated balanced 2²: df for A, B and AB are each 1; pure error df=4(r−1); total df=4r−1.
For a full 2^k design, each of the 2^k−1 factorial effects has 1 df; treatment df=2^k−1.
In a balanced design, orthogonal factorial contrasts partition treatment SS into non-overlapping components.
Inspect interaction/cell means before interpreting averaged main effects.
cards: Average response at A+ minus A−
Difference between the two simple A effects
Independent experimental unit at same treatment combination
Interaction first; then simple and marginal effects

tricks.why: Factorial means every selected factor-level combination is included in a full factorial.
Average over the other factor(s); do not confuse a main effect with a simple effect.
If the A effect differs between B− and B+, A and B interact.

shortcuts: For a 2² table, calculate the four cell means first; marginal means then give main effects directly.
Use a difference-in-differences for AB: (A+−A− at B+)−(A+−A− at B−).
For a full 2^k design, treatment df is 2^k−1; each named factorial effect has one df.
remember: A significant interaction changes the interpretation: explain how treatment effects vary across the other factor's levels.
Balanced replication makes the standard factorial contrasts orthogonal and gives a clean treatment/error decomposition.
traps: Calling a repeated measurement on the same experimental unit an independent replicate.
Interpreting a zero average main effect as proof that the factor has no effect at any level of the other factor.
Confusing the AB interaction contrast with the average main effect of A or B.

scenes.title: Why study factors together?
scenes.objective: Define factors, levels, treatment combinations and factorial structure.
body: A factor is a controllable explanatory variable, such as temperature, pressure, fertiliser type or machine speed. A level is a selected setting of that factor. A treatment combination specifies one level of every factor in the experiment.

A factorial experiment studies the combinations together. This reveals not only how each factor changes the response on average, but also whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of another. That dependence is an interaction.

items.ask: What is a treatment combination in a two-factor experiment?
items.recall: One selected level of factor A paired with one selected level of factor B.
refresh: For a 2×3 design there are six combinations.
The combination, not an isolated factor level, is the treatment applied to an experimental unit.
A full factorial includes every combination of the chosen levels.

items.ask: Why is factorial experimentation often more informative than changing one factor at a time?
items.recall: It can estimate interactions while studying several factors efficiently.
refresh: Separate one-factor studies can miss dependence between factors.
A factorial layout allows main effects and interactions to be estimated from one coordinated experiment.
Efficiency depends on the design, resources and scientific question.

items.ask: What is an interaction between two factors?
items.recall: The effect of one factor changes across levels of the other factor.
refresh: Compare the simple effect of A at each level of B.
If those simple effects differ, the additive model does not describe the response pattern fully.
The interaction contrast is the difference between the simple effects; it is not the same as either marginal main effect.
This distinction is essential before interpreting a factorial ANOVA table.

ask.q: What is the main decision or result in “Why study factors together?”?
ask.nudge: State the rule in your own words, then connect it to the calculation or design example in this scene.

scenes.title: A 2² design has four treatment combinations
scenes.objective: Construct the complete two-factor, two-level layout.
body: Let factor A be temperature (low/high) and factor B be pressure (low/high). A full 2² factorial contains all four combinations: A−B−, A+B−, A−B+ and A+B+. The signs are coded levels, not positive or negative responses.
The four combinations should be randomly allocated to experimental units. If each combination is independently applied r times, there are 4r experimental units in a balanced replicated design.

scenario.teaser: A process engineer varies temperature and pressure, each at two settings.
scenario.title: Count the runs before collecting data
body: The engineer wants to assess both temperature and pressure and whether the temperature effect changes with pressure. Both factors have two settings.
The full factorial requires 2×2=4 distinct treatment combinations. With three independent replicates per combination, the experiment uses 12 experimental units.
The three observations at each combination are genuine replicates only if treatment is independently assigned to three experimental units, rather than three readings from one unit.
scenario.q: How many combinations and experimental units are required with three replicates?
scenario.answer: Four combinations; 4×3=12 independently treated experimental units.

ask.q: Why does a 2² factorial have four combinations rather than two?
ask.nudge: List the two A levels against both B levels.

scenes.title: Main effects are marginal average effects
scenes.objective: Calculate the main effects from the four cell means.
body: The main effect of A compares the average response at A+ with the average response at A−, averaging over both B levels. The main effect of B is defined similarly, averaging over A.
With cell means y₁₁, y₂₁, y₁₂ and y₂₂, the A effect is [(y₂₁+y₂₂)−(y₁₁+y₁₂)]/2. The B effect is [(y₁₂+y₂₂)−(y₁₁+y₂₁)]/2. These are differences of marginal means.

ask.q: If A+ has average 16 and A− has average 10, what is the main effect of A?
ask.nudge: High-level marginal mean minus low-level marginal mean.

scenes.title: Interaction: the effect changes across another factor
scenes.objective: Interpret the AB interaction using simple effects.

blocks.body: At B−, compare A+ with A−. At B+, make the same comparison. These are the two simple effects of A.
AB interaction contrast = (A effect at B+)−(A effect at B−). If this is non-zero, the A effect changes with B.
A strong interaction can make a marginal main effect misleading. Inspect cell means or simple effects; the same factor may help at one level and hurt at another.

ask.q: At B−, A increases the response by 4; at B+, A increases it by 10. What is the interaction contrast?

scenes.title: The 2³ factorial and the hierarchy of effects
scenes.objective: Count effects and treatment degrees of freedom in a three-factor design.

blocks.body: Three two-level factors A, B and C create 2³=8 combinations. A full factorial includes all eight.
There are three main effects A, B, C; three two-factor interactions AB, AC, BC; and one three-factor interaction ABC. Total treatment df=8−1=7.
A three-factor interaction means a two-factor interaction itself changes across the level of the third factor. Interpretation should be guided by the scientific question and adequate replication.

ask.q: How many non-empty factorial effects occur in a full 2³ design?
ask.nudge: Eight treatment combinations minus one grand-mean degree of freedom.

scenes.title: Worked 2² example: calculate the effects
scenes.objective: Compute two main effects and one interaction from replicated cell means.
scenes.problem: A process is tested at low/high temperature (A) and low/high pressure (B). The four cell means are A−B−=9, A+B−=13, A−B+=11 and A+B+=19.
hints: Compute A marginal means from the two cells at each A level.
Compare the simple A effects at B− and B+.
scenes.answer: The marginal main effects are A=6 and B=4; the AB difference-in-differences is 4.
scenes.check: The A effect changes from 4 at B− to 8 at B+; hence the interaction is non-zero.

scenes.title: Factorial ANOVA partitions treatment variation
scenes.objective: Relate factorial effects to treatment, error and total degrees of freedom.

blocks.body: There are four combinations and r replicates per combination. Total N=4r; total df=4r−1; treatment df=3; pure error df=4(r−1).
A, B and AB each have one df. In a balanced design, the three orthogonal factorial contrasts partition treatment SS: SS_Treat=SS_A+SS_B+SS_AB.
For each effect, F=MS_effect/MS_error. Under the standard fixed-effects normal model, the denominator is the pooled within-combination error mean square.

ask.q: For r=3 replicates per combination, what are the total and error df?

scenes.title: Complete replicated 2² ANOVA
scenes.objective: Verify sums of squares, degrees of freedom and F ratios exactly.
scenes.problem: Two observations are recorded at each combination: A−B− (8,10), A+B− (12,14), A−B+ (10,12), A+B+ (18,20).
hints: Grand mean is 13; each cell has two observations.
scenes.answer: The ANOVA decomposition is 120=72+32+8+8; with df (1,1,1,4,7), the F ratios are 36, 16 and 4.
scenes.check: All sums of squares add to 120; all degrees of freedom add to 7.

ask.q: Why does the treatment SS equal 112 in the worked example?
ask.nudge: Add the three orthogonal effect components: 72, 32 and 8.

scenes.title: Interpret an interaction before the main effects
scenes.objective: Choose a scientifically meaningful interpretation when simple effects differ.
scenes.problem: A chemical additive increases yield by 2 units at low temperature but decreases yield by 3 units at high temperature.
hints: The simple effects have opposite signs.
Averaging them can conceal the reversal.
Describe the interaction and conditional effects.

solution.math: At low temperature: +2. At high temperature: −3.
The additive's effect depends on temperature and reverses direction.

scenes.answer: There is an interaction: the additive increases yield at low temperature but decreases it at high temperature. Report the conditional effects rather than relying only on the marginal main effect.
scenes.check: A marginal average of −0.5 would conceal the opposite simple effects.

scenes.title: Exam drill: degrees of freedom in 2³
scenes.objective: Calculate factorial and residual degrees of freedom.
scenes.problem: A full 2³ factorial has four independent replicates at each of its eight combinations.
hints: Error df is number of combinations times (r−1).
scenes.answer: Treatment df=7, error df=24 and total df=31.
scenes.check: The three df components (7+24) reconcile to total 31.

scenes.title: Common factorial-design traps
scenes.objective: Avoid misreading interactions, combinations and replication.

items.claim: A 2² full factorial has four treatment combinations.
items.why: Two levels for each of two factors give 2×2=4 combinations.

items.claim: A main effect is the effect of A at only the low level of B.
items.why: That is a simple effect; the main effect averages over B levels.

items.claim: A non-zero AB interaction means the A effect differs across B levels.
A full 2³ design has seven non-empty factorial effects.
items.why: Three main effects, three two-factor interactions and one three-factor interaction.

items.claim: Three readings from one experimental unit always count as three independent replicates.
items.why: Independent treatment assignment to experimental units, not repeated readings, defines replication.

scenes.intro: Mark each statement TRUE or FALSE. Read the reason after submitting all verdicts.

scenes.title: Transfer: choose the right factorial interpretation
scenes.objective: Apply factorial logic to a new applied experiment.

scenario.teaser: A hospital compares two training methods and two reminder systems.
scenario.title: Two factors, one response
body: A hospital evaluates training method (standard/intensive) and reminder system (text/no text). Every combination is assigned to independent teams, with equal replication.
The intensive method improves performance substantially when text reminders are absent, but adds little when reminders are present. The reminder effect also differs by training method.

The design should estimate both main effects and their interaction. If the interaction is important, the team-specific cell means and simple effects explain the result more clearly than a single average effect.
scenario.q: Which design and which effect should receive special attention?
scenario.answer: A replicated 2² factorial design; examine the training-by-reminder interaction and then interpret simple effects.

hints: Identify the number of factors and the levels of each factor.
Compare the effect of training at each reminder level.
If the simple effects differ, interpret the interaction before relying on marginal effects.
scenes.problem: A hospital compares two training methods and two reminder systems. The intensive method improves performance substantially when text reminders are absent, but adds little when reminders are present. Identify the factorial design and the effect that needs careful interpretation.

solution.math: Two factors, each at two levels: a replicated 2² factorial.
The training effect is large without reminders and small with reminders.
The training-by-reminder interaction matters; report simple effects and cell means.

scenes.answer: Use a replicated 2² factorial and interpret the training-by-reminder interaction through simple effects.

scenes.title: Factorial experiments: final revision
scenes.objective: Consolidate the design, effect and ANOVA rules.
body: A full factorial studies every combination of the chosen factor levels. For 2² there are four combinations; for 2³ there are eight. Main effects are marginal average differences, while interactions describe changes in one factor's effect across levels of another.

For a balanced replicated 2² design, A, B and AB each have one df; with r replicates per combination, error df=4(r−1), total df=4r−1. Orthogonal contrasts partition treatment SS into A, B and AB components.

When interaction is substantial, interpret cell means and simple effects. Replicate independently, randomise treatment allocation, and distinguish repeated measurements from independent experimental units.
